speechtext: What about the post office?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: I shall come to that later on. I contend that a government-owned monopoly of broadcasting in Canada would be one of the most dangerous things that could happen. Mr. Priestley has something to say on that point. I find it in a little pamphlet of his entitled "If I ran the B.B.C." In this instance, of course, he speaks about the British Broadcasting Corporation. I understand that excerpts from the pamphlet were read into the record of the committee which sat last year. This was published originally in the London Sunday Dispatch, and reprinted, through special arrangement with the distinguished author, by the National Association of Broadcasters, Washington, D.C.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: A private broadcasting organization.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
It might be, but I do not think that affects the material embodied in the pamphlet. Mr. Priestley said:
What is really wrong with the B.B.C. is that it represents a monopoly. No other broadcasting system is allowed. Competition is barred.
Radio Broadcasting

There is only one runner in the race. So that the listener here in England is told to like it or lump it. . . . Supposing there was only one firm of publishers, one great book shop, and all the theatres were controlled by one man?
The very idea chills me. I should loathe such a situation. One bad quarrel, and I might find myself thrown clean out of work.
Of course that is Mr. Priestley's style of writing. He goes on to say:
But the man who lives by broadcasting in England must please the B.B.C. or starve. He cannot say, "I'll walk across to your competitors". There are no real competitors. The B.B.C. stands alone.
For some kinds of service, competition is wasteful and absurd. You do not want two post-
I suppose he means post offices.
-telegraph or telephone systems in a country. I doubt if there is very much gain even in having competing railway systems.
But the B.B.C. is in another category of service, where, in my opinion, a monopoly is wrong. For it sets out now to be an entertainer, and nobody wants entertainment on a "take it or leave it" basis.
There is a world of difference between a variety show and a penny stamp. You do not want to pick and choose a penny stamp. One new one is as good as another. But you do want to pick and choose your entertainment.
In this connection may I say something right along this line. I fear lest the day should come when the government-owned radio corporation will have a monopoly on broadcasting in Canada. One reason for this is the value of propaganda. No one will deny that radio' is a powerful medium of propaganda, but may I say that propaganda is not the exclusive right of any set of minds or of any school of thought. Nor should it be the exclusive right of those who can afford to pay for it. The solution of this last problem presents some difficulty. I would be loathe to see the day when this powerful medium of propaganda is in the hands of a monopoly, whether it be privately or government owned.
I should like to read from a clipping taken from the'Ottawa Citizen of February 16, 1943, reporting an address by Doctor James S. Thomson given in Toronto. The press dispatch reads:
Dr. James S. Thomson, general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to-day told members of the Canadian association of broadcasters that "we must beware that we don't sell our medium to any political party or power."
I agree with that, but I imagine that Doctor Thomson is using the word "political" in its, shall I say, vulgar sense. Used in its true sense, "political" simply means the science of government. Someone has said
I Mr. Hansell.]
that a word is known by the company it keeps, and I am afraid that in the past this word has not kept very good company. The article continues:
"Radio doesn't belong to anyone," he said before a meeting of the association's three day annual convention. "It belongs to the people and with them it should remain. I can say, so far as the CBC is concerned, that wre don't propose to sell out to anyone. But we have to recognize the need of the political leaders to use this medium in a democratic country and we have got to strike some common means for that use."

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: What does he mean by political leaders?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I do not know what he means. The article continues:
Doctor Thomson said that the radio men of Canada had to "fight for the freedom of religion, education and entertainment."
I should like to comment here that radio broadcasting in Canada does not maintain freedom of religion over the air. I know of one religious organization in particular-and there may be others-which is not permitted to broadcast. The last sentence of this press dispatch is very important in my opinion, and it deserves considerable criticism. It reads:
He described polities and economics as "dangerous" fields for radio, adding: "And no one is more aware of that danger than I am."
It will be noted that he puts politics and economics in the same basket and describes these two as being dangerous fields for radio. I should like to ask, who are to be the judges of what is dangerous in politics and economics? Who is to be the judge of what is right and what is wrong? We must discover the right and the wrong of both politics and economics. Are these judges to be trained in all the arts and sciences, in economics and political economy? If so, in what school of political science and economics are they to be trained? I imagine that when many people talk of what is dangerous, they are not so much concerned with what is dangerous for the country as they are with what is dangerous for the status quo which has proved long since to have failed.
I come again to this matter of propaganda. Somebody is to judge what is right and what is wrong, and I contend that in a democracy the most competent to judge what is right and what is wrong are the people. If we are to have some sort of governing body, self-imposed judges, who perhaps are servants of bygone days, to say what is right and what is wrong, then the propaganda machine of Canada in the hands of such men is indeed tremendously dangerous. This country still

Radio Broadcasting
believes in free speech, and if there is one institution in the world that should guard this priceless heritage of liberty it is a government-controlled body. Any attempt whatsoever to stifle free speech would not be well received by a democratic people. Propaganda, let me say, is largely concerned with ideas, and it is impossible to kill a new idea. You may deny it a channel of expression; you may deny your particular propaganda machine to this idea; but the idea, if right, remains, and sooner or later will find its expression even though it be through sheer force of circumstances.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that rules and regulations are necessary in broadcasting. I recognize that there must be some ruling concerning the kind of language that shall be used and that there should be regulations to do away with abuses. The governors or the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have perhaps done a good piece of work along that line. But we have the defence of Canada regulations and the criminal code, which I think will take care pretty well of everything that is or may be dangerous to the country. Absolutely free course should be given to the discussion of subjects, no matter how controversial they may be.
I do not wish to be misunderstood in what I am about to say. There are people in Canada who believe that the only way in which real change can come both politically and economically is by force. I think the government has had some little trouble in days gone by with people who hold that view and who contend that the powers that be are so entrenched that they will not permit of change. But for a government-controlled radio to stifle or refuse the expression of new ideas would tend only to confirm such a contention. The best way to give the lie to such a contention is for the various mediums of propaganda-I refer here particularly to radio-to encourage, and not stifle, the fullest and widest possible discussion of all subjects. As I said, I do not wish to be misunderstood. In the illustration that I have given I am not arguing a case for that group \yho may believe in the overthrow of the status quo by force. I am suggesting that I am arguing a case for the proper functioning of democracy. Mr. Priestley has something to say about that too. Here is a quotation from his book, "Out of the People". He is talking about the old financial system being scrapped and so forth, and asks why it has not been scrapped. This is what he says:
Because too many influential persons, in a position to sway government and control public
opinion, were directly interested in keeping the rotten old thing going; and unless this supreme racket is smashed, we shall be plunged again into the same whirlpool of overproduction, underconsumption, crazy competition, poverty and unemployment, revolution and war.
I know that Mr. Priestley does not agree with the idea of overthrowing government by force. My argument here is that under a proper functioning of democracy the people themselves should have free course to the mediums of propaganda that are in their midst. What would happen if there should be a government monopoly of radio in Canada? We would have a government monopoly of propaganda, and that is a most dangerous thing to anticipate. Speaking of propaganda,
I think we have come to a place in our thinking and in our history w'hen we do not know what to believe. I am quite certain that somebody lied a few years ago, or else they are lying now, because a few years ago the old propaganda machine got busy and pictured Russia and the political regime there as something terrible. It might be; Ido not know; I am not arguing pro or con. But that is what we were told a few years ago. And now what happens? The old propaganda machine begins to grind again and the picture changes. Instead of the political regime in Russia being a hideous thing we are now told it is a glorious thing, and the idea is catching on. I say that somebody must have lied then, or somebody is lying now. You cannot have it both ways. That is propaganda. I do not think there has been any change. The alignment of nations has changed. Force of circumstances may have brought about change. And so I say, Mr. Speaker, that if the channels of propaganda are closed to the people by self-imposed judges who attempt to say what is right and what is wrong, that is a most dangerous thing for democracy.
I would suggest that no powerful group of propagandists have the right to propagate that which is untrue, while a less powerful group or a more insignificant group are stifled and stopped from propagating that which is right. The only way in which that can be overcome is to give access to the mediums of propaganda to the people for free discussion, unhindered, and let the people judge for themselves.
There are just one or two other observations I should like to make in closing. I am not a harsh critic of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Personally I am fairly well satisfied with it, but I believe that in days to come this organization can be improved. In this connection we must safeguard the people's rights. As my leader has said, we must be assured of freedom of expression.
Radio Broadcasting

I commend the work of the corporation along many lines. The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar has referred to one or two programmes which I myself like, such as Fibber McGee and Molly, which is a clean and humorous feature. Not everything which is spoken of as humorous is humorous to me, and I do not admit to being backward as a judge of humour. Some things which are called humorous are tremendously "corny" to me.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: What does "corny" mean?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
If my hon. friend asks me what is the meaning of "corny", I assume he has not been running with the people who can tell him what it means, for if he had he would have heard the word a good many times. It is one of those words which fit a situation without being explained.
I commend the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for some of its Sunday programmes. I suppose that, being in the profession I am in, I pay some little attention to that. The Church of the Air is, I think, commendable; it gives the people an opportunity to hear some of the country's outstanding clergymen. I would also compliment the corporation upon their Bible dramas which come over the air on Sunday mornings. I have listened to many of them; they are well dramatized and exceptionally well written. But, as I remarked in the committee last year, speaking for a tremendous minority, I do not relish the comedian programmes coming on the air on Sundays. Perhaps it is my background; perhaps it is my training, but I believe we should be better off were we to "remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy." I know that some of these Sunday evening programmes, in particular Charlie McCarthy and Fred Allen, are immensely popular, but I wish they were transferred to some other night in the week. Out west a favourite programme comes on at a time which is not the best for those who desire 1 to attend some place of worship in the evening.
With these comments, I find that my time is gone. May I repeat that I hope the organizational set-up of broadcasting in Canada will be such that a responsible body, not the present board of governors-which may continue to function, if so desired, to govern the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-but a body which might be known as the board of radio commissioners, shall be appointed to govern all radio in Canada, the government-owned corporation as well as the privately-owned interests.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, in his remarks as to the board of governors being in a dual position, in that they control not 
only the broadcasting corporation but all radio in Canada. It is to some extent the same situation as though the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways were in control of all railway activities in the country. I entirely agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) that something should be done in this regard; it is definitely a difficulty in connection with broadcasting.
The hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) in the course of his remarks indicated that there was some political significance in the request of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) for representation of labour and agriculture on* the board of governors. Well, all one has to do is to pick up a list of the board in order to decide if there is any political significance in the appointments. I venture to say that eveiy one of them is a dyed-ind-he-wool Grit.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: True.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
That is true.
Another observation which I think is called for is, what kind of corporation* have we in the present board? Is it an emanation of the crown; is it a separate organization, or what is it? Certainly it is in control of all broadcasting in Canada. In view of that fact, have we not the right to examine the minutes of the corporation? What rights have we as a committee as far as they are concerned?
For years we have been very jealous to preserve the freedom of the press. Now we have a government-owned radio existing alongside private radio. I agree in this regard with the hon. member who has just spoken, that a government monopoly is just as bad as a private monopoly. We should not allow radio to get to that stage. Unfortunately to-day the radio is in the hands of the government. It is not free with respect to all classes of people; it is in the hands of the government, and it is certainly used for Liberal political propaganda. There is no doubt about that.
The report of the committee shows very plainly what the committee felt. They held the governors of the broadcasting corporation responsible for the things which were found existing at that time which were not right. They said:
The board of governors, therefore, cannot escape responsibility for allowing the condition of affairs disclosed by the investigation to continue.
The report castigating the board for their actions was very strong. Naturally one would have thought that when the board received that report they would have resigned in a body.

Radio Broadcasting

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Not a
chance.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
But the board of
governors did not resign in a body. They did something else; they appointed one of their own members, who is just as responsible as the rest of them for the state of affairs which the committee found to be at fault, to be temporary general manager. What a spectacle! All these things had been found to be going on all these years under the administration of the board, and they take one of their own men and appoint him general manager of the corporation. It does not seem to me that this was the right thing to do.
The new general manager then proceeds to make a speech, or, as a matter of fact, two speeches. I should like to know why he should make such a speech. In the speech he made in Halifax on January 22, 1943, he is reported as saying:
"Among my chief distinctions," Doctor Thomson said, without naming the person to whom he was referring, ". . . has been that of providing the theme for the 'swan song' of an elder Canadian statesman, who spent the greater proportion of his last public address as leader of a great political party in demonstrating the wickedness of the CBC in general, and of its general manager in particular."
Everyone knows who the gentleman was to whom reference was made. The speech which he delivered was a statesmanlike address, and it was certainly correct in what it stated. Why, then, should the general manager of this corporation take it upon himself to sneer at a man in public life? I think it was, to say the least, quite uncalled for. In his speech Doctor . Thomson goes on to say:
It was alleged that we were simply a creation of the government, providing opportunities for political leaders to ingratiate themselves with the Canadian people through the medium of radio.
Well, as far as the government is concerned, that is perfectly true. The ministers of the crown and the Prime Minister have the radio at their command at any time, and! their speeches are not censored. They can say what they like; yet when a great statesman who is retiring from public life, a great statesman so far as Canada is concerned, wishes to use the air, and when his supporters wish him to use it, he is deprived of that right. But the government can use the air. Is it only the ministers of the crown who are Simon pure and can, therefore, speak over the air without attacking or abusing or doing anything like that? Could not the leader of a great party do the same?
Let me come to something else. Our leader was refused the air because there could not be anything controversial on the radio; yet one
of our commentators, "Professor" Watson Thompson in the west, in a speech which he delivered, certainly stated many things that were controversial. In one part of his speech he said that Great Britain was in the position of an exploiter and oppressor of India and that Canada should set Britain right by taking her place in the ranks of those who would show Britain the right way to deal with India. In other words, according to him, Great Britain has been the oppressor all these years. He goes on to say that Great Britain betrayed Czechoslovakia, Spain and China. So far as India is concerned, I wonder if this gentleman knows what he is talking about. Some of our members of parliament connected with the empire parliamentary association know a little about the situation, and they are aware of the difficulties that Great Britain has had to cope with for so many years; and yet a "professor" from the west comes along and makes such a speech over the radio without having anything said to him, having it paid for by the government of this country.
There are many other observations I should like to make, but I will conclude with this remark. What we want is fair play in connection with the radio. We want equal rights. As members of the House of Commons we have some rights in connection with the radio. Why should certain national figures be chosen to make speeches over the radio, while other men in political life are not allowed to speak; that is, except members of the government? I repeat, we want fair play. Are we to understand that only those people are national heroes who are either in the government or not in politics at all? I shall have more to say about this later on.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): Mr. Speaker, at this very late hour, may I crave the indulgence of the house and ask that I be given just two or three minutes in which to make one or two statements. I have heard with much interest what has been said this afternoon by hon. gentlemen, and I appreciate their points of view. The purpose of my motion is to have this committee set up, and I shall not burden the house with any lengthy statement. I desire, however, to make two observations. To the best of my knowledge and belief there is no reason for anyone in this house to say that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is dominated or influenced in any degree by the government.

May I ask a question? Is there not intelligent anticipation of the government's wishes on the part-of the governors?

Mr. LaFLECHE: I think I can give a very-fair answer to that question. Sometimes I think their anticipation has not been intelligent. To the best of my knowledge, I repeat, there has been no political interference with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the new general manager has been so kind as to take it upon himself to say on several occasions, in one part of Canada or mother, that there is no such interference.

speechtext:

rcer said it to the minister? That is more -,o the point.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes, he has, after his speeches, because on one or two occasions I questioned him as to why he had made such statements, and he said it was true and it pleased him to say so.
Another point is with respect to the composition of the board of governors. I take friendly issue with the hon. leader of the opposition when he questions the appointment of a lady to the board of governors.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Not as a lady.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The lady named recently to the board of governors replaced another lady who had resigned on account of ill health. I would not be a party to allowing the board of governors to continue without at least one member being a lady.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I was just sorry she was not a farmer; that was all.
Mr. LaFLECHE: May I say this, that this lady was reported to me to be eminently qualified in all matters relating to farm problems, life on a farm, and the requirements of the farming population.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to set up the committee; not, as -far as I can see, to discuss the merits of the broadcasting corporation here. There is another place for that, namely, before the committee. By reason of that fact, and because at the very beginning of this session the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made the statement to the house that there would be a select committee on radio broadcasting, which I, like all others, am anxious to see created, I shall not detain the house any longer, but will close, having in mind the opportunity that will be mine later on to speak on the matter in the committee.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 6.05 p.m.

Monday, May 10, 1943
